You shouldn't trust any news source completely. They are all subject to pressures and prejudices from reporters, editors, owners, etc. What you should focus on is reading critically and from different sources so that you can form your own opinion.

This is what I've been asking myself. My solution is to read multiple sites and try to form my own conclusion, being aware of biases I may have gotten from the diction/slant of the source. If you feel you're being told what to think and just want facts, Google is your best friend. Try extracting pure facts from an article and check them against your own research and see how your opinion holds up. 

The issue is that I feel people aren't looking for facts when they are reading. Confirmation bias seems to be the main goal. And with news, you're going to visit a site that aligns with your ideology mostly. 

Off the top of my head, I visit sites like Uproxx, The Daily Beast, The Daily Dot, Pacific Standard, Medium, Buzzfeed (their long-form is pretty good, they had a great piece on anxiety I can't locate....just ignore posts like 71 Ways You JUST KNEW You And Your BFFL Were TOTES Brangelina!) and a few others I can't. Not all of these are news, and aren't the best for unbiased, but I feel I get a large view of the internet that day. I like them because they are approachable. 

I use a modified new tab page (I use Humble New Tab) on Chrome and put the websites I know I like there so I'm not grasping for a source I feel I can rely on. I HIGHLY recommend doing this. 

Otherwise, it's up to you to see what sources speak to you the best.

The only organized form of news I get is from RSOE, they have an android app too. Other than that, be interested in current events and get many different sources, primary sources are key. And think critically.

Like others say in this thread are saying, you shouldn't trust any one source completely. I use Reuters along with YourNewsWire, and RT. As a general tip, I always try to find primary documents on a story, but these sites are definitely better than the mainstream news channels.
